note: All story, chat, hint, card and debrief text. Story beats: max 12 words each, under 300 words in total. Story plus chat: under 650 words. The science event, teacher and crew are fictional. Sara Seager and Chris Hadfield are named as inspiration only: no portraits, no quotes, no endorsement.

story.text: Mississauga, Ontario. Night. You are ten and love strategy games.
Today a science fair talked about two people from Ontario.
Chris Hadfield, a Canadian astronaut, commanded the Space Station.
Sara Seager, born in Toronto, studies planets around other stars.
You wonder: could I build a home on the Moon?
So you draw a Moon base on your map.
The Lab and Rover Garage must wait. Power and people first.
Your teacher says: A civilization needs more than buildings.
It needs people, resources, science and a plan.
You study astronomy at the University of Toronto.
You earn a PhD. You never stop asking questions.
You train as an astronaut. This is a dream, not a promise.
Years later, the Moon fills your window.
I drew this when I was ten. It is missing things.
Commander, your crew is ready. Build them a home.
Radio from a class in Mississauga: How do you breathe?
Good question. Build Life Support to make air.
A long shadow is coming. Less sun means less power.
First harvest! The crew shares fresh greens.
Mission control: solar particle warning. The Sun still shines.
Yuki is outside, far from base.
Particles are here. Keep the crew in a powered Shelter.
All clear. The storm has passed.
The crew gathers at the window.
Sunlight creeps over the ridge. Solar power climbs.
Earth hangs low above the horizon.
Priya hands you an old photo: your first drawing.
I used to build this world on a computer.
Now we are building it together.
On Earth, a new kid opens Blueprint v2.
Yuki walks out to study old rocks.
Mission control: the Sun is very active.
Years later, a new rocket waits.
Next stop: Mars.
We land at Jezero crater. Long ago, it held a lake.

chat.line: Power is like water in a tank. Never let it empty.

replies.answer: Switch off what can wait. Air never waits.

chat.line: The battery is draining. Something must switch off.

replies.answer: The Greenhouse can rest. Life Support cannot.

chat.line: Two batteries! Now we can save energy for later.
The Shelter needs extra power. Check the battery now.

replies.answer: No. A warning is not a power cut.

chat.line: My seeds need soil, light, water and power.
Look, tiny sprouts! We recycle most of their water.

replies.answer: Water is hard to bring here. Every drop counts.

chat.line: First harvest! Real food, grown on the Moon.
Short on power? Let my plants rest. People come first.

replies.answer: Plants can wait a few hours. We cannot.

chat.line: These rocks are older than any city on Earth.

replies.answer: Maybe ice, hiding in the dark craters.

chat.line: My rover found soft soil for Mateo.

replies.answer: Ice in dark craters. Clay on Mars.

chat.line: I am far from base. Should I come back?

replies.answer: Okay. Call me if it gets worse.

chat.line: Safe inside. Thank you for watching over us.
You called me in first. I will not forget that.

replies.answer: That is why we follow you.

chat.line: That storm was scary. Call me sooner next time?

cards.title: Sun at home, Sun at the pole
cards.text: Mississauga gets about five times more sunlight energy in June than in December.
cards.text2: At the Moon's poles the Sun is never more than 1.5 degrees above the horizon, so shadows are long.
cards.source: NASA POWER climatology; NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4893)
cards.label: NASA-derived, simplified

cards.title: Sunny ridges, dark craters
cards.text: On this map the sunniest ridge is lit about 70% of the time. Some crater floors nearby are never lit.
cards.text2: The brightness of each tile comes from a real map of the Moon's south pole.
cards.source: LRO LOLA illumination map (Mazarico et al. 2011)
cards.label: simplified from real map

cards.title: Why grow plants in space?
cards.text: Plants can provide food, produce oxygen, and recycle carbon dioxide.
cards.text2: Over three million students have taken part in the Tomatosphere program.
cards.source: Canadian Space Agency, Tomatosphere page. © Canadian Space Agency
cards.label: CSA-derived

cards.title: Far from the grocery store
cards.text: On the Moon or Mars, astronauts will need to be more self-sufficient.
cards.text2: Supply trips will be rare, so crews must grow food.
cards.source: Canadian Space Agency, Growing healthy food in space. © Canadian Space Agency
cards.label: CSA-derived

cards.title: A real reading from the Space Station
cards.text: A Space Station dosimeter measured about 4 microgray per hour during this real storm week.
cards.text2: The Station is in low Earth orbit. This is NOT a Moon dose. The game's safety meter is made up.
cards.label: NASA-derived

cards.title: Ice in the dark
cards.text: Some craters near the Moon's poles never see the Sun. They can trap water ice.
cards.text2: In 2009, NASA's LCROSS found water in one of them, Cabeus. Not every dark crater has ice.
cards.source: NASA NSSDC, Ice on the Moon; NASA LCROSS mission
cards.label: NASA-derived

cards.title: Less sunlight on Mars
cards.text: Sunlight on Mars is about 43% as strong as on Earth. Panels make less power.
cards.text2: A Mars day, called a sol, lasts about 24 hours 40 minutes. The game skips Mars nights.
cards.label: NASA-derived; game power is softened

cards.title: Jezero crater
cards.text: NASA's Perseverance rover landed in Jezero crater in 2021. Long ago it held a lake.
cards.text2: This map uses real heights measured by the MOLA laser on Mars Global Surveyor.
cards.source: MGS MOLA MEGDR (NASA PDS); NASA Mars 2020 mission
cards.label: simplified from real map

cards.title: Making oxygen from Mars air
cards.text: Mars air is 95% carbon dioxide. NASA's MOXIE made oxygen from it on Mars.
cards.text2: At its best, MOXIE made 12 grams of oxygen an hour. In total it made 122 grams.
cards.source: NASA JPL, MOXIE completes Mars mission (6 Sept 2023); NASA Mars Fact Sheet
cards.label: NASA-derived
